nameStory: The spring salamander gets its name from its love of cool, clean spring waters where it makes its home. Its scientific name tells an even more interesting story - 'Gyrinophilus' means 'tadpole lover,' referring to how these salamanders spend an unusually long time as gilled larvae in the water. They're also sometimes called purple salamanders because 'porphyriticus' refers to the color of porphyry, a beautiful purple stone.
description: The spring salamander is one of New England's larger salamanders, with a robust body and relatively long tail. These amphibians have smooth, moist skin that ranges from salmon-pink to reddish-brown, often with a purplish tint that gives them their alternate name of purple salamander. They have prominent eyes and a broad head that helps distinguish them from smaller stream salamanders. As lungless salamanders, they breathe entirely through their skin, which must stay moist to work properly.

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Noticeably chunky and substantial - one of the larger salamanders you'll encounter in New England streams, with a thick body that feels solid when gently handled

idTips.label: Color/Pattern
idTips.description: Salmon-pink to reddish-brown skin with a distinctive purplish cast, especially on the back and sides, giving it an almost iridescent quality in good light

idTips.label: Skin
idTips.description: Smooth, wet skin that feels slippery to the touch - noticeably more robust and less delicate-feeling than smaller stream salamanders

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Large, prominent eyes that seem oversized for the head, often with a golden or bronze iris that catches the light

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in and around cold, clean springs and rocky streams, often hiding under large stones or logs near the water's edge where the ground stays consistently moist

habitat: Spring salamanders prefer cool, clean streams and springs in forested areas throughout New England's mountains and hills. Look for them under rocks and logs near cold-water sources, especially where springs emerge from hillsides or where small rocky streams flow through mature forest. They need consistently moist conditions and high water quality, making them indicators of healthy aquatic ecosystems.

seasonality.spring: Active and easier to spot as they emerge from winter retreats. Look under stones near stream edges during mild, wet days when they're hunting for food.
seasonality.summer: Most active during cooler parts of the day and after rain. Check under rocks and logs close to cold springs and stream edges, especially during humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to move to deeper retreats. Good time to find them under larger rocks and logs that will provide winter protection.
seasonality.winter: Hidden deep under rocks, logs, or in underground spaces near water sources. Rarely seen unless you're doing serious rock-turning on warmer winter days.

funFact: Spring salamanders are the bullies of the salamander world - they're cannibalistic predators that regularly hunt and eat other salamanders, with smaller species like two-lined salamanders making up nearly half their diet in some areas!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with red salamanders, but spring salamanders are chunkier with a more purplish tint, while red salamanders are more slender and bright red. Remember: 'Spring salamanders are stout, red salamanders are svelte.'
contextualKnowledge: The name 'purple salamander' can cause confusion since they're not actually purple - the name comes from their scientific name referring to purple porphyry stone, describing their subtle purplish cast rather than a true purple color.
compareHints: Spring salamanders are the only species in their genus found in New England, making them unique among our lungless salamanders. Compared to other large stream salamanders like the red salamander, spring salamanders are noticeably more robust and thick-bodied, with that distinctive purplish tinge. They're also more aggressive predators than most of their relatives, actively hunting other salamanders rather than focusing mainly on small invertebrates.
